content: Earwax, medically referred to as cerumen, is a yellowish, waxy substance secreted in the ear canal of humans and many other mammals. It serves several critical functions, including cleaning and lubricating the ear canal, as well as providing protection against bacteria, fungi, and insects. However, excessive or impacted cerumen can press against the eardrum or block the external auditory canal, potentially impairing hearing. Cerumen is produced in the outer third of the cartilaginous portion of the ear canal. It is a mixture of viscous secretions from sebaceous glands and less-viscous secretions from modified apocrine sweat glands. The primary components of earwax are the final products of the HMG-CoA reductase pathway, including squalene, lanosterol, and cholesterol. There are two genetically determined types of earwax: the wet type, which is dominant, and the dry type, which is recessive. Asians and Native Americans are more likely to have the dry type (gray and flaky), while Caucasians and Africans are more likely to have the wet type (honey-brown to dark-brown and moist). Anthropologists have used cerumen type to trace human migratory patterns, such as those of the Inuit. The difference in cerumen type is linked to a single nucleotide polymorphism in the ATP-binding cassette C11 gene. This mutation also reduces sweat production, which may have been advantageous for the ancestors of East Asians and Native Americans who lived in cold climates. The cleaning of the ear canal occurs through a conveyor belt process of epithelial migration, aided by jaw movement. Cells formed in the center of the tympanic membrane migrate outward from the umbo to the walls of the ear canal and accelerate toward the entrance of the canal. Cerumen in the canal is carried outward, taking with it dirt, dust, and particulate matter. Jaw movement helps dislodge debris attached to the canal walls, increasing the likelihood of its expulsion. Lubrication provided by cerumen prevents desiccation, itching, and burning of the skin within the ear canal, a condition known as asteatosis. The lubricative properties arise from the high lipid content of the sebum produced by sebaceous glands. In wet-type cerumen, these lipids include cholesterol, squalene, and various long-chain fatty acids and alcohols. While earlier studies found little evidence of an antibacterial role for cerumen, more recent research has demonstrated its bactericidal effects on certain bacterial strains. Cerumen has been shown to reduce the viability of a wide range of bacteria, including Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and various strains of Escherichia coli, sometimes by up to 99%. Additionally, the growth of two fungi commonly associated with otomycosis was significantly inhibited by human cerumen. Excessive cerumen can obstruct sound transmission in the ear canal, leading to conductive hearing loss. It is also estimated to cause 60–80% of hearing aid malfunctions. Jaw movement, such as chewing gum or talking, can aid the ear's natural cleaning process. If this is insufficient, general practitioners commonly use warm water syringing to remove cerumen. Otolaryngologists may prefer the curette method when the ear canal is partially occluded and the material is not adhering to the canal's skin. For individuals with wet-type earwax, softening the wax before removal is often necessary. This process, known as cerumenolysis, involves the use of a cerumenolytic agent introduced into the ear canal. Common home remedies include olive oil, while other agents include sodium bicarbonate, glycerine, and commercially available solutions like Cerumol and Cerumenex. A cerumenolytic should be applied 2–3 times daily for 3–5 days before extraction. Studies suggest that a 10% sodium bicarbonate solution is more effective than several commercial solutions and organic liquids. Docusate, a detergent found in laxatives, has also been shown to be effective. Once the cerumen is softened, it can be removed via irrigation. This involves gently streaming warm water, saline, or a sodium bicarbonate solution into the ear canal. The water flows out along the canal floor, carrying wax and debris with it. Patients generally prefer the irrigation solution to be warmed to body temperature to avoid dizziness. Recommendations for water temperature range from 37°C to 38°C. Irrigation may need to be repeated several times, and it is better to irrigate gently over a longer period than to apply excessive force. This procedure can also be performed at home using a self-use ear irrigation syringe with a right-angle tip. The curette method involves physically dislodging and scooping out earwax using an ear pick. In Western countries, this method is typically performed by healthcare professionals, while in East Asia, where dry-type earwax is common, it is often done at home. Dry earwax is easier to remove as it tends to fall out in large pieces or flakes. The removal of cerumen is not without risks. Complications can include otitis externa, pain, vertigo, tinnitus, and eardrum perforation. A survey of British general practitioners found that only 19% always performed the procedure themselves, with many delegating it to practice nurses, some of whom had no formal training. Failure to remove all wax accounted for approximately 30% of complications associated with the procedure. Claims arising from ear syringing mishaps make up about 25% of total claims received by New Zealand's Accident Compensation Corporation ENT Medical Misadventure Committee. Cotton swabs (Q-tips) are generally not recommended for ear cleaning, as they can push wax further into the canal and may perforate the eardrum if used carelessly. Abrasion of the ear canal, particularly after water exposure, can lead to infection. Cotton swabs should only be used to clean the external ear. Ear candling, a folk medicine practice, involves placing a hollow candle in the ear canal and lighting it, with the belief that rising hot air will pull out wax and toxins. However, scientific evidence does not support its efficacy, and it poses risks such as hot wax dripping into the ear, causing pain and potential hearing damage. Studies have found that ear candling has no real effect on earwax removal and can result in ear injuries. In whales, earwax accumulates annually, forming one to four layers per year depending on the species. These layers can be counted post-mortem to determine the whale's age, similar to tree ring dating. For further reading, a comprehensive review of earwax physiology and pathophysiology can be found in a 1997 article by Roeser and Ballachanda.
